arXiv:1508.00951v3 [math.CO] 29 Sep 2015

On Ryser’s Conjecture for Linear
Intersecting Multipartite Hypergraphs

Research supported by ARC grant DP120100197
Nevena Francetić Note:  School of Mathematical Sciences, Monash University Victoria 3800 Australia.    Sarada Herke 22footnotemark: 2    Brendan D. McKay Note: Research School of Computer Science, Australian National University, Canberra, ACT 0200, Australia    Ian M. Wanless22footnotemark: 2
Abstract

Ryser conjectured that τ⩽(r−1)​ν\tau\leqslant(r-1)\nu for rr-partite hypergraphs, where τ\tau is the covering number and ν\nu is the matching number. We prove this conjecture for r⩽9r\leqslant 9 in the special case of linear intersecting hypergraphs, in other words where every pair of lines meets in exactly one vertex.

Aharoni formulated a stronger version of Ryser’s conjecture which specified that each rr-partite hypergraph should have a cover of size (r−1)​ν(r-1)\nu of a particular form. We provide a counterexample to Aharoni’s conjecture with r=13r=13 and ν=1\nu=1.

We also report a number of computational results. For r=7r=7, we find that there is no linear intersecting hypergraph that achieves the equality τ=r−1\tau=r-1 in Ryser’s conjecture, although non-linear examples are known. We exhibit intersecting non-linear examples achieving equality for r∈{9,13,17}r\in\{9,13,17\}. Also, we find that r=8r=8 is the smallest value of rr for which there exists a linear intersecting rr-partite hypergraph that achieves τ=r−1\tau=r-1 and is not isomorphic to a subhypergraph of a projective plane.

1 Introduction

A hypergraph HH is a set of non-empty subsets, variously called lines, edges or hyperedges, of a finite underlying vertex set V⁡(H)V(H). The degree of a vertex v∈V⁡(H)v\in V(H), denoted deg⁡(v){\rm deg}(v), is the number of lines in HH that contain vv. A hypergraph is rr-uniform if every line contains exactly rr vertices. Thus a 22-uniform hypergraph is simply a graph.

Covers and matchings in hypergraphs are widely studied [6]. A cover of a hypergraph HH is a set of vertices C⊆V⁡(H){C}\subseteq V(H) such that every line of HH contains at least one vertex of C{C}. The covering number of HH, denoted τ⁡(H)\tau(H), is the minimum size of a cover of HH. A matching in HH is a set of pairwise disjoint lines of HH and the matching number of HH, denoted ν⁡(H)\nu(H), is the maximum size of a matching in HH. Most hypergraphs in this paper are intersecting, meaning that every pair of lines meets in at least one vertex; equivalently ν=1\nu=1.

The covering number and matching number of a hypergraph are related. First, for every hypergraph, ν⩽τ\nu\leqslant\tau since each cover contains at least one vertex from each line in any given matching. Second, for every rr-uniform hypergraph, τ⩽r​ν\tau\leqslant r\nu since a cover can be obtained from the union of the lines in a maximal matching; this bound is sharp and is achieved, for example, by projective planes of order r−1r-1.

A hypergraph is rr-partite if its vertex set can be partitioned into rr sets, called sides, such that every line consists of exactly one vertex from each side. Hence every rr-partite hypergraph is necessarily rr-uniform. An rr-partite hypergraph can be constructed from a projective plane of order r−1r-1 by removing a single vertex vv and the rr lines through vv. The resulting hypergraph 𝒫r′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{r} is called a truncated projective plane and the rr sides of 𝒫r′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{r} are defined by the sets of vertices on each of the removed lines. Our notation hides the fact that there may be non-isomorphic choices for the structure of 𝒫r′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{r}, but the distinction between the different choices will not matter in our work.

The following famous conjecture is due to Ryser [9].

Conjecture 1.1.

Every rr-partite hypergraph with covering number τ\tau and matching number ν\nu satisfies τ⩽(r−1)​ν\tau\leqslant(r-1)\nu.

Ryser’s Conjecture is far from being resolved. When r=2r=2, the conjecture is König’s Theorem for bipartite graphs, which is also equivalent to Hall’s Theorem (see e.g. [12]). Using topological methods, Aharoni and Haxell [4] proved a hypergraph generalisation of Hall’s Theorem and Aharoni [2] used this result to prove Conjecture 1.1 for r=3r=3. Conjecture 1.1 was proved for intersecting rr-partite hypergraphs with r⩽5r\leqslant 5 by Tuza [11]. Haxell and Scott [7] built on this result to prove that for r⩽5r\leqslant 5, there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that τ<(r−ϵ)​ν\tau<(r-\epsilon)\nu for all rr-partite hypergraphs.

In this paper, we prove another restricted version of Ryser’s Conjecture for small rr. A hypergraph is linear if each pair of lines meets in at most one vertex. Hence, in a linear intersecting hypergraph, each pair of lines intersects in exactly one vertex. In §2 we prove that Conjecture 1.1 holds for r⩽9r\leqslant 9 when HH is a linear intersecting hypergraph. The proof of the r=9r=9 case is computational.

In an intersecting rr-partite hypergraph each side is a cover and each line is also a cover. In [3] the following strenthening of Conjecture 1.1 is recorded. The conjecture is due to Aharoni, as are several generalisations that are also given in [3].

Conjecture 1.2.

An intersecting rr-partite hypergraph HH has a side of size at most r−1r-1 or a cover of the form e∖{v}e\setminus\{v\} for some e∈He\in H and v∈ev\in e.

In §3.1 we show that Conjecture 1.2 is false, by providing a counterexample when r=13r=13. Furthermore, in §3.3 we describe an infinite family of linear intersecting rr-partite hypergraphs with τ=r−2\tau=r-2, built from mutually orthogonal latin squares. Although this family of hypergraphs have covers consisting of an line with a vertex removed, they have the property that no minimal cover is contained within a line or a side.

In studying Conjecture 1.1 it is natural to investigate hypergraphs that achieve the equality τ=(r−1)​ν\tau=(r-1)\nu. A well-known infinite family of such hypergraphs with ν=1\nu=1 is the family of truncated projective planes 𝒫r′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{r} (where r−1r-1 is a prime power). Note that τ⩽r−1\tau\leqslant r-1 since each side of 𝒫r′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{r} has r−1r-1 vertices and τ⩾r−1\tau\geqslant r-1 since each vertex lies on r−1r-1 lines and the total number of lines is (r−1)2(r-1)^{2}. However, 𝒫r′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{r} has more lines than is necessary in the sense that many of its subhypergraphs achieve τ=r−1\tau=r-1. Conversely, we will report in §4 that for r⩽7r\leqslant 7 the only way to achieve τ=r−1\tau=r-1 in a linear intersecting rr-partite hypergraph is to take a subhypergraph of 𝒫r′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{r}. In particular, there are no linear intersecting 77-partite hypergraphs with τ=6\tau=6, since 𝒫7′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{7} does not exist. By contrast, it was shown in [1, 3] that there are non-linear intersecting 77-partite hypergraphs with τ=6\tau=6. We also describe in §3.4 a linear intersecting hypergraph having r=8r=8 and τ=7\tau=7 and which is not a subhypergraph of 𝒫8′\mathcal{P}_{8}^{\prime}. Moreover, in §3.2 we give examples of non-linear intersecting rr-partite hypergraphs with r∈{9,13,17}r\in\{9,13,17\} which have covering number r−1r-1.

1.1 Notation

We deal with rr-partite hypergraphs throughout. To avoid degeneracies we always assume that r⩾2r\geqslant 2 and that every vertex has positive degree. The sides of our hypergraphs are always denoted V0,V1,…,Vr−1V_{0},V_{1},\dots,V_{r-1} and we have V=∪i=0r−1ViV=\cup_{i=0}^{r-1}V_{i}. The covering number, matching number, minimum degree and maximum degree of a hypergraph are denoted by τ\tau, ν\nu, δ\delta and Δ\Delta, respectively. The number of lines in a hypergraph HH is denoted hh or |H||H|. We often use discrete interval notation [n1,n2]={n1,n1+1,n1+2,…,n2}[n_{1},n_{2}]=\{n_{1},n_{1}+1,n_{1}+2,\dots,n_{2}\}, where n1n_{1} and n2n_{2} are two integers and n1⩽n2n_{1}\leqslant n_{2}.

2 Ryser’s conjecture for linear intersecting hypergraphs

In this section we prove that Conjecture 1.1 holds for all linear intersecting hypergraphs with at most nine sides. We begin by establishing some properties of a hypothetical counterexample.

2.1 General properties

Lemma 2.1.

Let HH be an intersecting rr-partite hypergraph with τ⁡(H)=r\tau(H)=r. Then

  • (i)

    Each side of HH has size at least rr.

  • (ii)

    Each vertex of HH has degree at least 22.

  • (iii)

    Each line of HH contains at most one vertex of degree 22.

Proof.

Each side is a cover so it contains at least τ⁡(H)\tau(H) vertices, hence (i) holds. If a vertex vv has degree 11 and ℓ\ell is the line containing vv, then ℓ\{v}\ell\backslash\{v\} is a cover of size r−1r-1, hence (ii) holds. Finally, if there is a line ℓ\ell containing distinct vertices uu and vv of degree 22, then we get a cover of size r−1r-1 by taking ℓ\{u,v}∪{x}\ell\backslash\{u,v\}\cup\{x\}, where xx is a vertex in the intersection of the (at most) two lines other than ℓ\ell that meet {u,v}\{u,v\}. Therefore, (iii) is proved. ∎

Lemma 2.2.

Let HH be an intersecting rr-partite hypergraph with τ⁡(H)=r\tau(H)=r. Then Δ⩾4.\Delta\geqslant 4. Furthermore, if HH is linear, then Δ⩽r−2\Delta\leqslant r-2.

Proof.

By Lemma 2.1, we may assume that δ⁡(H)⩾2\delta(H)\geqslant 2. Suppose there are hh lines in HH. If we count the lines which intersect a given line, we find that h⩽(Δ−1)​r+1h\leqslant(\Delta-1)r+1 with equality only if HH is Δ\Delta-regular. If we count the lines incident with a side that contains a vertex of degree Δ\Delta, we find that h⩾2​(r−1)+Δh\geqslant 2(r-1)+\Delta, with equality only if all other vertices on that side have degree 22. The above observations together show that Δ⩾4\Delta\geqslant 4.

Now suppose that HH is linear and let vv be a vertex of degree Δ\Delta. Without loss of generality, assume that vv is on side V0V_{0} and let u∈V0∖{v}u\in V_{0}\setminus\{v\} (such a uu exists, since τ⁡(H)>1\tau(H)>1). Any line ℓ\ell through uu meets the lines through vv in Δ\Delta distinct vertices on sides other than V0V_{0}, since HH is linear and intersecting. Hence Δ⩽r−1\Delta\leqslant r-1. If Δ=r−1\Delta=r-1 then side V1V_{1} has at most r−1r-1 vertices. Indeed, ℓ\ell cannot contain any vertex on side V1V_{1} other than the vertices on lines through vv. As this is true for any line ℓ\ell which does not contain vv, there can only be r−1r-1 vertices in V1V_{1}, which means that τ⁡(H)⩽r−1\tau(H)\leqslant r-1. We conclude that Δ⩽r−2\Delta\leqslant r-2. ∎

In a linear intersecting rr-partite hypergraph with τ=r\tau=r, we have 4⩽Δ⩽r−24\leqslant\Delta\leqslant r-2, by Lemma 2.2. Substituting Δ∈{4,5,6}\Delta\in\{4,5,6\} into (2.1)(\ref{e:lem}), yields an immediate contradiction. Hence:

Corollary 2.4.

If there exists a linear intersecting rr-partite hypergraph HH such that τ⁡(H)=r\tau(H)=r, then Δ⁡(H)⩾7\Delta(H)\geqslant 7.

Corollary 2.5.

Conjecture 1.1 holds for all linear intersecting rr-partite hypergraphs when r⩽8r\leqslant 8.

2.2 Linear intersecting 𝟗9-partite hypergraphs

In this subsection we prove that a linear intersecting 99-partite hypergraph has covering number at most 88. For a potential counterexample HH, let h=|H|h=|H| be the number of lines in HH and ε:=|V⁡(H)|−r2⩾0\varepsilon:=|V(H)|-r^{2}\geqslant 0. First, we demonstrate some further properties that such a hypergraph would have, if it were to exist. Note that we may assume that Δ=7\Delta=7, given Corollary 2.4 and Lemma 2.2.

Lemma 2.6.

If HH is a linear intersecting 99-partite hypergraph with Δ=7\Delta=7 and τ=9\tau=9, then h⩾39h\geqslant 39.

Proof.

Let uu be a vertex of degree Δ=7\Delta=7, and without loss of generality, assume that u∈V0u\in V_{0}. Let AA be the set of vertices that lie on lines through uu in the remaining eight sides. Then |A|=8⋅7=56|A|=8\cdot 7=56. Let B=V⁡(H)∖(V0∪A)B=V(H)\setminus(V_{0}\cup A). Then |B|⩾16|B|\geqslant 16.

Let ℓ\ell be a line through a vertex in BB. Then ℓ\ell is incident with a vertex other than uu in side V0V_{0} and it intersects all seven lines incident with uu. That is, |ℓ∩A|=7|\ell\cap A|=7 and |ℓ∩B|=1|\ell\cap B|=1. Since every vertex in BB has degree at least 22, there are at least 2​|B|⩾322|B|\geqslant 32 such lines. Therefore, h⩾7+32=39h\geqslant 7+32=39. ∎

By (2.6)(\ref{e:quadratic}),

h2−(Δ​r+Δ/2+2​r)​h+3​r2​Δ⩽−3​Δ​ε.h^{2}-(\Delta r+\Delta/2+2r)h+3r^{2}\Delta\leqslant-3\Delta\varepsilon. (2.7)

This inequality has no integer solution for hh when ε⩾5\varepsilon\geqslant 5 if r=9r=9 and Δ=7\Delta=7. Otherwise, together with Lemma 2.6, we obtain that hm​i​n​(ε)⩽h⩽hm​a​x​(ε)h_{min}(\varepsilon)\leqslant h\leqslant h_{max}(\varepsilon) where hm​i​n​(ε)h_{min}(\varepsilon) and hm​a​x​(ε)h_{max}(\varepsilon) are as follows:

Lemma 2.7.

If HH is a linear intersecting 99-partite hypergraph with Δ=7\Delta=7 and τ⁡(H)=9\tau(H)=9, then for every pair of degree 77 vertices on different sides there is a line of HH that contains both vertices.

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary that v0v_{0} and v1v_{1} are degree 7 vertices on sides V0V_{0} and V1V_{1}, respectively, which do not lie on a common line. Let e1,…,e7e_{1},\dots,e_{7} be the lines which contain v0v_{0} and f1,…,f7f_{1},\dots,f_{7} be the lines which contain v1v_{1}. For every i,j∈[1,7]i,j\in[1,7], lines eie_{i} and fjf_{j} meet at a vertex in one of the last seven sides V2,…,V8V_{2},\dots,V_{8}.

Define V0′=V0∖((∪iei)∪(∪ifi))V_{0}^{\prime}=V_{0}\setminus\bigl((\cup_{i}e_{i})\cup(\cup_{i}f_{i})\bigr) and V1′=V1∖((∪iei)∪(∪ifi))V_{1}^{\prime}=V_{1}\setminus\bigl((\cup_{i}e_{i})\cup(\cup_{i}f_{i})\bigr). Since |V0|⩾9|V_{0}|\geqslant 9, there exists y∈V0′y\in V_{0}^{\prime}. Any line ℓ\ell through yy intersects each of f1,…,f7f_{1},\dots,f_{7} in the last seven sides and thus also intersects each of e1,…,e7e_{1},\dots,e_{7} in the last seven sides. Hence ℓ\ell contains a vertex in V1′V_{1}^{\prime}. By symmetry, all lines through V1′V_{1}^{\prime} contain a vertex in V0′V_{0}^{\prime}. Let GG be the bipartite graph induced on V0′∪V1′V_{0}^{\prime}\cup V_{1}^{\prime} by HH. Then GG inherits from HH the properties of having minimum degree at least 22 and no line between vertices of degree 22. Therefore GG has at least 55 vertices and at least 66 lines. It follows that ε⩾3\varepsilon\geqslant 3 and hence h⩽46h\leqslant 46, from (2.7).

We have already encountered 20 distinct lines of HH, namely e1,…​e7,f1,…,f7e_{1},\dots e_{7},f_{1},\dots,f_{7} and at least 66 lines through V0′V_{0}^{\prime}. Let BB be the set of vertices in the last seven sides which do not lie on any of these 20 lines. Then |B|⩾14|B|\geqslant 14, since BB includes at least two vertices from each of V2,…,V8V_{2},\dots,V_{8}. Let x∈Bx\in B, and let gg be a line through xx. Since gg intersects each line e1,…,e7e_{1},\dots,e_{7}, it follows that g∩B={x}g\cap B=\{x\}. However xx has degree at least 22. Therefore h⩾20+2​|B|⩾48h\geqslant 20+2|B|\geqslant 48, which is a contradiction. ∎

Remark.

Although the proof of Lemma 2.7 does not completely generalise to larger rr, it does demonstrate that if HH is a linear intersecting rr-partite hypergraph with Δ=r−2\Delta=r-2, τ=r\tau=r and ϵ⩽2\epsilon\leqslant 2, then each pair of degree Δ\Delta vertices on different sides lie on a common line.

2.2.2 Pairwise conditions

Our next goal is to verify which degree sequences are feasible. We assume that hh and ε\varepsilon are given, and that D=[d2,d3,…,d7]D=[d_{2},d_{3},\dots,d_{7}] is a degree sequence in 𝒟⁡(h,ε)\mathcal{D}(h,\varepsilon). Suppose that there exists HH, a linear intersecting hypergraph with r=τ=9r=\tau=9, Δ=7\Delta=7 on r2+εr^{2}+\varepsilon vertices with hh lines and the given degree sequence. For every t∈{1,2,…,|𝒮⁡(h,ε)|}t\in\{1,2,\dots,|\mathcal{S}(h,\varepsilon)|\}, let xtx_{t} denote the number of sides of type tt that are contained in HH. For every t∈{1,2,…,|ℒ⁡(h)|}t\in\{1,2,\dots,|\mathcal{L}(h)|\}, let yty_{t} denote the number of lines of type tt that are contained in HH. Then xtx_{t} and yty_{t} are non-negative integers which satisfy some obvious necessary conditions listed by equations (2.8)–(2.11). Equation (2.12) is a double count of pairs of vertices of degree ii and lines on which these vertices lie, for i∈[2,7]i\in[2,7]. Since HH is a linear intersecting hypergraph, no pair of vertices is contained on two lines. This condition is given by equations (2.13)–(2.15), depending on whether we count pairs of vertices having the same degree, or pairs of vertices with different degree. Putting all of these conditions together, we formulate an integer program on variables xtx_{t} and yty_{t}.

Two vertices are neighbours if there is a line containing both of them. Observe that, for each vertex vv in a given side, the number of neighbours of vv which have degree jj is at most the total number of degree jj vertices in the remaining sides, for j∈[2,7]j\in[2,7]. Since every line contains exactly one vertex in each side, each side is incident with as many lines of a type tt as there are lines of type tt present in the hypergraph, which is given by (2.20). Finally, (2.21) is a double count of pairs of lines of type tt and vertices of degree ii incident with these lines.

Theorem 2.8.

For 2⩽r⩽92\leqslant r\leqslant 9 every linear intersecting rr-partite hypergraph has covering number at most r−1r-1.

3 Hypergraph constructions

In this section we describe several hypergraph constructions that are of interest. First we define some additional notation. Let HH be an rr-partite hypergraph. In each side VkV_{k}, we label the vertices by (k,0),(k,1),…,(k,|Vk|−1)(k,0),(k,1),\dots,(k,|V_{k}|-1), which we abbreviate to 0,1,…,|Vk|−10,1,\dots,|V_{k}|-1 when the side is clear from context. We say that a vertex (k,l)∈Vk(k,l)\in V_{k} is at level ll in side VkV_{k}. We denote a line ee in HH by [l0,l1,l2,…​lr−1][l_{0},l_{1},l_{2},\dots l_{r-1}], where ee contains the vertex at level lkl_{k} in side VkV_{k}, where k∈[0,r−1]k\in[0,r-1]. When presenting a specific example, we omit the square brackets and commas to make the notation cleaner. The cyclic 11-shift of a line [l0,l1,l2,…,lr−1][l_{0},l_{1},l_{2},\dots,l_{r-1}] is the line [lr−1,l0,l1,…,lr−2][l_{r-1},l_{0},l_{1},\dots,l_{r-2}] and the cyclic tt-shift of a line ee, denoted ete^{t}, is the line obtained from ee by applying tt cyclic 11-shifts. In particular, e0=e=ere^{0}=e=e^{r}. An rr-partite hypergraph is cyclic if its automorphism group contains a cyclic subgroup of order rr acting transitively on the sides. A cyclic rr-partite hypergraph can be obtained by developing a set of starter lines by cyclic shifts.

3.1 A counterexample to Conjecture 1.2

In this subsection we give a counterexample to Conjecture 1.2.

For at least one value of rr there is an intersecting rr-partite hypergraph HH such that each of its sides has size rr and e∖{v}e\setminus\{v\} is not a cover for any e∈He\in H and any v∈ev\in e.

3.2 Cyclic intersecting hypergraphs with 𝝉=𝒓−𝟏\tau=r-1

Next we give an example of a cyclic intersecting rr-partite hypergraph which has covering number r−1r-1 for r∈{9,13,17}r\in\{9,13,17\}. The methodology for building these hypergraphs is similar to the construction given in the proof of Theorem 3.1. However, in each case below the hypergraph we construct is non-linear.

Lemma 3.2.

Let (r,s)∈{(9,4),(13,5),(17,6)}(r,s)\in\{(9,4),(13,5),(17,6)\}. Then there exists a cyclic intersecting rr-partite hypergraph HH such that HH has s​rsr lines and τ⁡(H)=r−1\tau(H)=r-1.

Proof.

3.3 Linear intersecting hypergraphs built from latin squares

Next we describe a family of linear intersecting rr-partite hypergraphs which do not have a minimal cover that consists of a single side or that consists of a subset of a line.

A latin square of order nn is an n×nn\times n array of nn symbols such that each symbol appears exactly once in each row and exactly once in each column. If LL is a latin square, L⁡[r,c]L[r,c] denotes the symbol in row rr and column cc of LL. A pair of latin squares of order nn are orthogonal if, when the two squares are superimposed, each of the n2n^{2} possible ordered pairs of symbols occurs exactly once. A set of latin squares is called mutually orthogonal if each pair of latin squares in the set are orthogonal. For more on latin squares, see [12].

Lemma 3.3.

If there exist kk mutually orthogonal latin squares of order n⩾3n\geqslant 3, then there exists a linear intersecting (n+2)(n+2)-partite hypergraph HH with τ⁡(H)=k+1\tau(H)=k+1 such that no side or subset of a line is a minimal cover.

Proof.

Let L0,…,Lk−1L_{0},\dots,L_{k-1} be kk mutually orthogonal latin squares of order nn. Assume that each LiL_{i} has [0,1,…,n−1][0,1,\dots,n-1] as its first row. For i=0,1,…,k−1i=0,1,\dots,k-1, let MiM_{i} be the column inverse of LiL_{i}, that is, Mi​[r,c]=sM_{i}[r,c]=s if and only if Li​[s,c]=rL_{i}[s,c]=r. Since each LiL_{i} has its first row in reduced form, each MiM_{i} has symbol 00 on the main diagonal. Set M0′=M0M_{0}^{\prime}=M_{0} and for i=1,…,k−1i=1,\dots,k-1 let Mi′M_{i}^{\prime} be the latin square obtained from MiM_{i} by replacing symbol 00 with symbol n+i−1n+i-1.

Next we define the lines of an (n+2)(n+2)-partite hypergraph HH. Let V0,…,Vn+1V_{0},\dots,V_{n+1} be the sides of HH. Sides V0,…,VnV_{0},\dots,V_{n} each have n+k−1n+k-1 vertices and side Vn+1V_{n+1} has n+1n+1 vertices. If a line [l0,l1,…,lr−1][l_{0},l_{1},\dots,l_{r-1}] is a concatenation of two lists, we use the notation [l0,…,li]⊕[li+1,…,lr−1][l_{0},\dots,l_{i}]\oplus[l_{i+1},\dots,l_{r-1}].

For i=0,…,k−1i=0,\dots,k-1 define Ei:={Mi′​[x]⊕[i,x]:0⩽x⩽n−1}E_{i}:=\{M_{i}^{\prime}[x]\oplus[i,x]:0\leqslant x\leqslant n-1\}, where Mi′​[x]M_{i}^{\prime}[x] is row xx of the latin square Mi′M_{i}^{\prime}. Further, define E∗:={[x,x,…,x,k+x−1,n]:1⩽x⩽n−1}E^{*}:=\{[x,x,\dots,x,k+x-1,n]:1\leqslant x\leqslant n-1\}.

It is straightforward to check that each line in EiE_{i} intersects each line in E∗E^{*} exactly once, and that the lines in E∗E^{*} meet each other exactly once. Since Mi′M_{i}^{\prime} is a latin square, two distinct lines in EiE_{i} intersect only at the vertex (n,i)(n,i). We next show that lines of EiE_{i} and EjE_{j} also intersect linearly for i≠ji\neq j. Consider a line ℓ1=Mi′​[x]⊕[i,x]∈Ei\ell_{1}=M_{i}^{\prime}[x]\oplus[i,x]\in E_{i} and a line ℓ2=Mj′​[y]⊕[j,y]∈Ej\ell_{2}=M_{j}^{\prime}[y]\oplus[j,y]\in E_{j} where i≠ji\neq j. Since LiL_{i} and LjL_{j} are orthogonal latin squares, there is a unique cell (r,c)(r,c) where Li​[r,c]=xL_{i}[r,c]=x and Lj​[r,c]=yL_{j}[r,c]=y. If x=yx=y, then r=0r=0 and Mi​[x,x]=Mj​[x,x]=0M_{i}[x,x]=M_{j}[x,x]=0, and thus, by the relabelling of symbol 00 in M1′,…,Mk−1′M_{1}^{\prime},\dots,M_{k-1}^{\prime}, the lines ℓ1\ell_{1} and ℓ2\ell_{2} intersect only at the vertex (n+1,x)({n+1},x). If x≠yx\neq y, then r≠0r\neq 0 and thus Mi′​[x,c]=r=Mj′​[y,c]M_{i}^{\prime}[x,c]=r=M_{j}^{\prime}[y,c] and therefore the lines ℓ1\ell_{1} and ℓ2\ell_{2} intersect only at the vertex (c,r)(c,r). It follows that H=E∗∪E0∪E1∪⋯∪Ek−1H=E^{*}\cup E_{0}\cup E_{1}\cup\dots\cup E_{k-1} is a linear intersecting (n+2)(n+2)-partite hypergraph with k​n+n−1kn+n-1 lines.

Since HH has maximum degree nn and k​n+n−1kn+n-1 lines, no set of kk vertices is a cover. It is straightforward to check that the vertices at levels 0,1,…,k−10,1,\dots,k-1 of side VnV_{n} together with the vertex (n+1,n)({n+1},n) form a cover of size k+1k+1. Therefore τ⁡(H)=k+1\tau(H)=k+1.

It is well-known that there are at most n−1n-1 mutually orthogonal latin squares of order nn (see e.g. [12]), so k+1⩽nk+1\leqslant n. Observe that for k⩾2k\geqslant 2 each side has size at least n+1n+1, whereas τ⁡(H)=2<n\tau(H)=2<n when k=1k=1. Hence, no side is a minimal cover. Also, since HH is linear and each line contains exactly one vertex of degree 11, it follows that the only covers which are subsets of a line have size at least n+1n+1. Thus, no side or subset of a line is a minimal cover of HH. ∎

The following corollary follows immediately from the existence of complete sets of mutually orthogonal latin squares of prime power orders [12].

Corollary 3.4.

If nn is a prime power then there exists a linear intersecting (n+2)(n+2)-partite hypergraph HH with τ⁡(H)=n\tau(H)=n such that no side or subset of a line is a minimal cover.

3.4 An 𝟖8-partite linear hypergraph with 𝝉=𝟕\tau=7

We close this section by giving a construction for an interesting 88-partite linear hypergraph ℋ38\mathcal{H}_{38} that achieves equality in Conjecture 1.1.

Let FF denote the Fano plane constructed by developing the triple {0,1,3}\{0,1,3\} modulo 77. Let GG denote the stabiliser of the point 00 in FF. Note that |G|=24|G|=24. Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} denote the set of 77-cycles obtained by conjugating the cycle (0123456)(0123456) by elements of GG.

For each permutation p∈𝒞p\in\mathcal{C} we add one line to ℋ38\mathcal{H}_{38} which includes the vertex (i,p⁡[i])(i,p[i]) for i∈[0,6]i\in[0,6]. If p1,p2∈𝒞p_{1},p_{2}\in\mathcal{C} then p1−1​p2p_{1}^{-1}p_{2} has at most one fixed point. We can make the lines corresponding to p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} meet on side V7V_{7} if and only if p1−1​p2p_{1}^{-1}p_{2} has no fixed points. This produces 88 vertices of degree 33 in V7V_{7}, and completes the description of the lines corresponding to the cycles in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Next we add two new vertices v1,v2v_{1},v_{2} to V7V_{7}. For each i∈[0,6]i\in[0,6] we put a line through v1v_{1} and the vertices (j,i)(j,i) for j∈[0,6]j\in[0,6]. For each i∈[0,6]i\in[0,6] we put a line through v2v_{2}, (i,i)(i,i) and all vertices (a,b)(a,b) for which {i,a,b}\{i,a,b\} is a triple of FF.

The construction just described results in ℋ38\mathcal{H}_{38}, which has 3838 lines and an automorphism group isomorphic to PSL(2,7)(2,7). For i∈[0,6]i\in[0,6] the vertex (i,i)(i,i) has degree 22. All other vertices on sides V0,…,V6V_{0},\dots,V_{6} have degree 66. On V7V_{7} the vertices v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} have degree 77 and the other 88 vertices have degree 33. Since V7V_{7} has 10 vertices it is clear that ℋ38\mathcal{H}_{38} is not isomorphic to a subhypergraph of 𝒫8′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{8}. Nevertheless, it is routine to check that ℋ38\mathcal{H}_{38} is a linear intersecting 88-partite hypergraph. Suppose that XX is a 66-cover of ℋ38\mathcal{H}_{38}. Then XX must include v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} since otherwise it cannot cover the lines through those vertices. The 2424 lines that avoid v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} induce a subhypergraph with maximum degree 44, which thus cannot be covered by fewer than 66 vertices. This contradiction shows that XX does not exist. Since V0V_{0} is a 77-cover, we must have τ⁡(ℋ38)=7\tau(\mathcal{H}_{38})=7.

Some further properties of ℋ38\mathcal{H}_{38} are discussed in the next section.

4 Computational results

In this section we describe a computational proof of the following result.

Theorem 4.1.

kick item 1 onto new line

  1. 1.

    For r⩽7r\leqslant 7 the only linear intersecting rr-partite hypergraphs to achieve equality in Ryser’s conjecture are subhypergraphs of 𝒫r′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{r}. In particular, there are none for r=7r=7.

  2. 2.

    No subhypergraph of ℋ38\mathcal{H}_{38} has τ=7\tau=7 and is isomorphic to a subhypergraph of 𝒫8′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{8}.

  3. 3.

    The smallest subhypergraph of ℋ38\mathcal{H}_{38} with τ=7\tau=7 has 2222 lines. The smallest subhypergraph of P8′P^{\prime}_{8} with τ=7\tau=7 also has 2222 lines.

Clearly, by part (1), every 77-partite linear intersecting hypergraph satisfies τ⩽5\tau\leqslant 5. There are a number of non-isomorphic ways to achieve τ=5\tau=5, including by the construction in Lemma 3.3. For 77-partite intersecting non-linear hypergraphs with τ=6\tau=6, see [1, 3].

Let HH be a 77-partite linear intersecting hypergraph with h=|H|h=|H| lines and τ⩾6\tau\geqslant 6. By an argument similar to the proof of Lemma 2.2 we know that Δ⁡(H)⩽6\Delta(H)\leqslant 6. We next argue that Δ⁡(H)⩾4\Delta(H)\geqslant 4. Let HH have xix_{i} vertices of degree i=1,…,Δi=1,\dots,\Delta. Note that no line of HH can include two vertices of degree 11, otherwise the remaining vertices on the line would provide a 55-cover. Hence x1⩽hx_{1}\leqslant h. Together with [3, Lem 2.1] and [3, Thm 2.7], we can then deduce that if Δ⩽4\Delta\leqslant 4 and x4⩽7x_{4}\leqslant 7 then x1=h=17x_{1}=h=17, x3⩾38x_{3}\geqslant 38 and hence x2<0x_{2}<0. It follows that Δ⩾4\Delta\geqslant 4. Also if Δ=4\Delta=4 then x4>7x_{4}>7 so some side of HH has at least 22 vertices of degree 44 on it.

We next describe the computation that established Part 1 of Theorem 4.1. By the above comments, we can split the problem for r=7r=7 into three subcases Δ=4\Delta=4, Δ=5\Delta=5 and Δ=6\Delta=6. We started with a vertex of degree Δ\Delta on side V0V_{0}. (In the Δ=4\Delta=4 case, we then added a second vertex of degree Δ\Delta to V0V_{0} in all possible ways up to isomorphism.) Subsequent lines were added one at a time, ensuring that all pairs of lines intersected in a single point and that the assumed maximum degree was not violated. After each line was added, we tested for isomorphism and kept only one representative of each isomorphism class. For isomorphism checking we converted the hypergraphs into vertex-coloured graphs and applied the software nauty [8]. For Δ=4,5,6\Delta=4,5,6 the largest hypergraphs we obtained had 16,25,1816,25,18 lines respectively. All hypergraphs that we built had a 55-cover, proving the claim that no linear 77-partite intersecting hypergraph achieves τ=6\tau=6.

For r⩽6r\leqslant 6, we performed computations as just described, except that there was no need to split the problem into subcases according to the maximum degree. Every hypergraph that we encountered could be extended to 𝒫r′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{r}.

For r⩾8r\geqslant 8 the above method is not practical for a complete enumeration. However, we did a partial enumeration and found a number of linear intersecting 88-partite hypergraphs that are maximal (no lines can be added), have τ=7\tau=7 and yet are not isomorphic to 𝒫8′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{8}. Most of these have the property that a few lines can be removed to get something isomorphic to a subhypergraph of 𝒫8′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{8}. However, the hypergraph ℋ38\mathcal{H}_{38} described in §3.4 seems to be of a very different nature, which is why we tested its properties more thoroughly.

In Table 1 and Table 2 all 2098796663 isomorphism classes of subhypergraphs of 𝒫8′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{8} with τ=7\tau=7, and all 17892655 isomorphism classes of subhypergraphs of ℋ38\mathcal{H}_{38} with τ=7\tau=7 are classified by their size. The tables were prepared by exhaustive enumeration, using a heuristic upper bound for the covering number to quickly eliminate most subhypergraphs with τ⁡(H)⩽6\tau(H)\leqslant 6, and employing nauty to remove isomorphs.

We end with an example of a subhypergraph of 𝒫8′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{8} that has 22 lines and τ=7\tau=7:
